clinicalPearls: A common cause of acquired conductive hearing loss in adults, often clustering in families with an autosomal dominant pattern and reduced penetrance
Progressive conductive loss results from abnormal bone remodelling fixing the stapes footplate at the oval window
Typical audiometric features include a low-frequency conductive loss and the Carhart notch, an apparent dip in bone conduction around 2 kHz that resolves after successful surgery
Cochlear (retrofenestral) otosclerosis can add a sensorineural component producing a mixed loss
Tympanometry usually shows a normal or shallow trace with absent acoustic reflexes rather than the effusion pattern of middle-ear disease
Options include hearing aids or stapes surgery (stapedotomy), with cochlear implantation reserved for advanced cochlear otosclerosis
Onset or progression is often noted during pregnancy, and there is a female predominance
reference.pathophysiology: Otosclerosis is a disorder of the otic capsule bone in which normal lamellar bone is replaced by disorganised, initially vascular spongy bone (otospongiosis) that later scleroses. When this remodelling involves the region of the oval window it progressively fixes the stapes footplate, impairing ossicular movement and producing conductive hearing loss; the Carhart notch reflects the mechanical effect of fixation on bone-conduction measurement rather than a true cochlear deficit. When the process extends into the cochlear endosteum (cochlear otosclerosis) it can damage the inner ear and add a sensorineural component. A familial predisposition with autosomal dominant inheritance and incomplete penetrance is well recognised, and hormonal factors are thought to influence progression.
additionalDifferentials: Enlarged vestibular aqueduct and other third-window lesions causing a pseudoconductive gap
Chronic otitis media and middle-ear effusion
Paget disease and other otic capsule dysplasias
additionalInvestigations: Pure-tone audiometry demonstrating conductive or mixed loss with a Carhart notch
Tympanometry and acoustic reflex testing to distinguish fixation from effusion
Speech audiometry to guide surgical versus amplification decisions
High-resolution temporal bone imaging to confirm otospongiotic foci and exclude third-window lesions
Cochlear function assessment where a mixed or sensorineural component is present
redFlags: A conductive gap with a normal tympanic membrane and normal tympanogram, which should prompt exclusion of a third-window lesion before surgery
Rapidly progressive sensorineural loss suggesting cochlear otosclerosis
Vertigo or a large air-bone gap pattern atypical for stapes fixation
Sudden hearing change after surgery indicating a complication
reference.prognosis: Progression is gradual, and stapes surgery closes the air-bone gap in the majority with durable benefit, while advanced cochlear otosclerosis may still be rehabilitated with cochlear implantation.
pitfalls: Operating on a presumed stapes fixation when the gap is actually from a third-window lesion such as canal dehiscence
Overlooking a coexisting sensorineural component from cochlear otosclerosis
Misreading absent reflexes and a shallow tympanogram as middle-ear effusion
Failing to counsel about the small risk of profound sensorineural loss after stapes surgery
